topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - nature.com
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context and digital competencies relevant to that region. Findings may have limited direct application to other geographic contexts or private sector AI literacy programmes, though core competency principles could be adaptable.
takeaways: European public health organisations can use this framework to identify and prioritise digital competencies their workforce needs, helping target training investments where gaps are greatest.
The framework offers a structured reference point for designing role-specific AI and digital literacy curricula in healthcare settings, reducing ad-hoc or fragmented upskilling efforts.

Consider how the competencies identified for public health translate to your sector — some may be directly applicable, while others may need contextualisation for organisational or private-sector AI development needs.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on public health faculty development; findings may not generalise across other academic disciplines or non-academic settings without further evidence.
takeaways: Faculty development programmes can shift mindsets from AI resistance to readiness; consider designing structured upskilling initiatives that address fears and build confidence rather than assuming adoption will follow naturally.

Targeted professional development for educators may be necessary before they can effectively teach AI literacy to others; invest in train-the-trainer approaches for your organisation's learning leaders.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis draws on global trends and client work, but specific findings may reflect consulting firm clientele (large enterprises) and may not generalise to small-to-medium businesses or non-Western contexts.
takeaways: Design AI upskilling programmes that address both technical skills and organisational change management, since AI adoption requires workforce transformation beyond technical training alone.

Identify role-level AI literacy needs early — some roles require deep AI expertise whilst others need functional understanding; tailor training intensity and content accordingly to avoid over- or under-investment.

Establish clear pathways for employee progression in AI roles and create opportunities to redeploy existing staff into AI-adjacent functions, which can reduce resistance and retain institutional knowledge during transformation.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - nature.com
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; unclear if findings extend to other age groups, educational systems, or geographic regions beyond the authors' context.
takeaways: AI literacy for younger learners should be embedded within a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught in isolation, helping students develop competencies across multiple interconnected skills.
Identify which specific AI competencies are developmentally appropriate for your learners' age group and integrate them into existing curriculum frameworks rather than creating standalone AI modules.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context; the four-domain model may be specific to academic management roles and may require adaptation for corporate or other organisational settings.
takeaways: Adopt a meta-skill framework for AI literacy that integrates multiple domains (e.g., technical understanding, ethical reasoning, strategic thinking) rather than treating AI competency as a single skill — this approach better supports leaders managing innovation across their organisations.

Use the four-domain model as a diagnostic tool to assess gaps in your team's AI literacy and design targeted upskilling interventions that address conceptual, practical, ethical, and strategic dimensions simultaneously.

articles.title: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — a discourse-based review examining conceptual and ethical dimensions of AI in person-centred care, but without empirical data on implementation outcomes across specific sectors or geographies.
takeaways: Identify and document potential pitfalls (e.g. algorithmic bias, loss of human judgment) before implementing AI tools in your organisation's people-centred processes to build stakeholder buy-in and risk mitigation strategies.

Use the framework to evaluate whether your AI applications genuinely enhance personalisation and individual autonomy, or risk reducing person-centred care to efficiency gains at the expense of human connection.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be fully assessed from the title and snippet alone. The research appears to examine psychological mechanisms (role ambiguity and self-efficacy) in AI adoption, but geographic scope, sample size, sector coverage, and methodology are unclear.
takeaways: Role ambiguity—uncertainty about how AI fits into job responsibilities—appears to be a key barrier to effective employee-AI collaboration; managers should clarify AI tools' intended use and integration points to reduce this friction.

Self-efficacy (confidence in using AI) operates as a separate pathway; consider pairing technical training with confidence-building opportunities, as both factors independently influence adoption outcomes.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - nature.com
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing roles and healthcare settings; may not generalise to other professional sectors or organisations with different AI implementation approaches. Longitudinal design strengthens causal inference within the studied sample.
takeaways: When introducing AI tools to clinical teams, actively protect and communicate how staff will retain decision-making authority and discretion — low perceived autonomy appears to undermine well-being gains even when AI readiness is high.

Design AI implementation programmes with explicit focus on maintaining or enhancing work autonomy; autonomy acts as a protective factor that translates readiness into positive outcomes like engagement and job satisfaction.
Conduct well-being assessments at multiple time points during AI rollout to monitor whether autonomy concerns emerge as barriers, allowing early intervention before morale and retention suffer.

articles.title: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents general observations about AI's impact on human cognition and skills from a US psychology organisation perspective, but lacks empirical data or specific sector/geographic validation. Insights may apply broadly but are not research-backed claims.
takeaways: Consider how your organisation's AI adoption might change the cognitive demands on employees — e.g. shift from execution to judgment and oversight — and plan reskilling accordingly.
Monitor whether increasing AI reliance is affecting critical thinking or problem-solving skills in your team; design learning interventions to maintain these capabilities rather than atrophy them.
Use this as a conversation starter with stakeholders about the psychological and developmental implications of AI integration, not just efficiency gains.

articles.title: Dimensions of artificial intelligence anxiety among employees in the age of innovation: a systematic review - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dimensions of artificial intelligence anxiety among employees in the age of innovation: a systematic review  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: High — systematic review synthesises evidence across multiple studies and geographies, though individual studies may vary in quality and geographic representation.
takeaways: Identify the specific dimensions of AI anxiety in your workforce (e.g., job security fears, skill obsolescence, loss of autonomy) to tailor targeted interventions rather than addressing anxiety generically.

Use findings on anxiety dimensions to design communication and training programmes that address root concerns — employees experiencing different types of AI anxiety may respond better to different support strategies.
Monitor and measure AI anxiety as a key psychological indicator alongside engagement and retention, as anxiety levels may predict adoption resistance or burnout in AI-enabled roles.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The theoretical framework (Automation–Augmentation Paradox) is broadly applicable, but findings' applicability across sectors, geographies, and organisational contexts cannot be assessed without methodological details.
takeaways: Generative AI in the workplace creates a dual dynamic: it can automate routine knowledge tasks (reducing skill use) while augmenting complex problem-solving—understanding which effect dominates in your context helps design appropriate training and role redesign.

Monitor how employees respond to AI assistance; passive automation can atrophy knowledge and critical thinking, whereas intentional augmentation strategies preserve and develop capability alongside AI tools.

articles.title: How rejection letters from AI recruiters shape recruiter's prestige and experienced respect - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How rejection letters from AI recruiters shape recruiter's prestige and experienced respect  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess without full article access. The snippet provides insufficient detail on sample size, geography, methodology, or sector to evaluate applicability to Australian organisational contexts.
takeaways: AI-mediated rejection communications may affect how candidates perceive recruiter credibility and organisational standing — consider whether your rejection process maintains human touchpoints that preserve candidate relationships and employer brand.

The framing and tone of automated rejection messages could influence candidate experience and future willingness to apply — audit your AI recruiter outputs for respectful language that acknowledges candidate effort, not just efficient screening.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner perspective likely draws on client work across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample details are not provided in the snippet. Findings may be most applicable to large organisations with resources for structured change programmes.
takeaways: Shift focus from 'AI adoption' (tool implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (behaviour change) — this reframe helps leaders identify which human behaviours and workflows need to change, not just which systems to deploy.

Design change interventions that build specific behaviours needed for AI success (e.g., comfort with ambiguity, collaborative problem-solving with AI) rather than treating AI rollout as a purely technical project.

Sequence behaviour change alongside system implementation — waiting until after deployment to address mindset shifts and skill gaps typically leads to lower adoption and performance, so embed behavioural change activities from the start.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - nature.com
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Limited — sample size and geographic scope not specified in snippet; findings based on cognitive appraisal theory and JD-R framework which have broad theoretical support, but real-world applicability depends on organisational context and employee demographics.
takeaways: AI awareness among employees can trigger job crafting (redesign of task scope and responsibilities) through two distinct pathways: stress appraisal and resource/demand perception — understanding which pathway is active in your team helps tailor change management strategies.

Use the dual-path insight to design targeted interventions: for employees experiencing stress from AI, focus on coping support and skill development; for those viewing AI as a resource opportunity, emphasise upskilling and task redesign autonomy.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and industry observations, but specific case studies and organisational contexts may not transfer directly to all sectors or organisation sizes.
takeaways: Structure AI transformation in three distinct phases (adoption, scaling, impact) rather than treating it as a single change initiative — this helps identify where your organisation sits and what capability-building activities are most urgent.

Map behaviour change interventions differently for each horizon: early adoption focuses on building literacy and reducing resistance; scaling requires embedding AI into workflows and roles; impact requires sustained culture shift and leadership modelling of AI-enabled decision-making.

Recognise that moving from adoption to impact typically stalls at the scaling phase — plan explicit interventions (training, process redesign, team restructuring) to prevent people reverting to pre-AI workflows once initial enthusiasm wanes.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford business school perspective without specified empirical data or geographic scope. Findings may reflect primarily US higher education and tech sector views.
takeaways: Identify which work tasks in your organisation are most vulnerable to AI displacement, then design upskilling programs that help employees transition to higher-value, uniquely human work (creativity, relationship-building, complex problem-solving).

Create feedback loops with employees about how AI tools are changing their roles, addressing concerns early rather than waiting for resistance to build — this helps prevent change fatigue and builds psychological safety around AI adoption.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to the full article, sample characteristics, geography, and methodology cannot be assessed. The theoretical framework suggests it may apply broadly to organizations adopting AI, but specific limitations are unknown.
takeaways: Employees respond to AI adoption through either approach behaviors (proactively adapting roles) or avoidance behaviors (resisting change) — understanding which response your team exhibits helps tailor support strategies.

Job crafting interventions (allowing employees to reshape their tasks and roles) may help convert avoidance responses into approach responses during AI transitions, reducing resistance and supporting capability development.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's analysis reflects practices across large multinational organisations, but may not fully represent small-to-medium enterprises or non-Western organisational contexts.
takeaways: Design AI adoption programmes that treat workforce capability building as central, not peripheral—integrate skills assessment, targeted training, and role redesign from day one rather than retrofitting learning after technology deployment.

Create clear career pathways that show employees how AI adoption affects their roles and growth opportunities; transparency about job transitions reduces resistance and helps people engage constructively with change.
Establish cross-functional change leadership teams that include frontline employees, not just executives, to surface real implementation barriers and build grassroots commitment to AI transformation.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — full methodology and sample details not provided. The finding may be limited by self-report bias and the specific population studied.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism appears to have surprising short-term romantic appeal, possibly because confidence and dominance can attract potential partners despite being traits associated with poor relationship outcomes.
This reveals a mismatch between what makes someone attractive initially and what makes them a good long-term partner — a counterintuitive insight into human mate selection.

The finding highlights how personality traits that seem obviously 'bad' can paradoxically confer advantages in competitive romantic contexts, challenging our assumptions about what people actually seek in dating.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Findings depend on sample composition and experimental design, which are not detailed in the snippet. Generalisability to real-world surprise events uncertain without additional methodological information.
takeaways: People with different personality traits remember surprising moments in distinctly different ways — some personalities may lock in vivid details while others might gloss over the unexpected.

Your personality isn't just about how you act; it shapes what your brain actually encodes and retrieves from surprising experiences, suggesting memory itself is a more personalised filter than we typically assume.

This challenges the common assumption that shocking or unexpected events create uniform, crystalline memories — in reality, your traits act like a lens that determines what 'sticks' when something surprises you.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline claims typically require access to the original research to assess methodological rigor, sample size, and whether findings have been replicated.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies consistently show structural and functional differences in psychopaths' brains, particularly in regions linked to emotion and impulse control — a genuinely striking finding that suggests personality traits have measurable neural correlates.

The framing of psychopathy as a 'shocking difference' reflects our enduring fascination with the neural basis of personality and morality, even though brain differences don't always predict behaviour in straightforward ways.

Popular headlines about 'shocking' brain scan findings often oversimplify complex neuroscience — the original study may have found nuanced patterns rather than clear-cut distinction, making this a good reminder to dig into source material before accepting headlines at face value.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings depend on the specific AI model used, the dataset of wine reviews analyzed, and whether patterns hold across different wine-drinking populations and cultural contexts.
takeaways: Wine review language reveals personality traits — the words people choose when describing wine appear to correlate with measurable personality characteristics, suggesting our everyday writing habits leak personality signals in unexpected places.

AI can spot personality patterns hidden in casual text — an algorithm picked up on personality-language links that might not be obvious to human readers, showing how machine learning can uncover subtle behavioral signatures in how we express preferences.

Your taste descriptions might say more about you than your taste — the way you evaluate wine (not just which wine you like) appears to be a personality fingerprint, which is a fun reminder that even seemingly objective reviews are deeply personal.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Findings likely generalise to Western populations with similar political systems, though twin study methodology assumes equal environments for monozygotic and dizygotic twins, which may not always hold. Geographic scope and sample characteristics not evident from snippet alone.
takeaways: Twin studies suggest authoritarian beliefs have a heritable component—counterintuitively, your political leanings may owe more to your genes than to your upbringing or current political environment.

The finding challenges the common assumption that authoritarianism is purely a product of parenting style or social conditioning, hinting instead at deeper biological or genetic underpinnings worth exploring.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — appears to be a multi-country study examining universal patterns in music preference and personality, suggesting findings apply across diverse cultures.
takeaways: People's music taste reveals consistent personality patterns worldwide — your Spotify playlist really might be a universal window into who you are, regardless of culture.
Musical preferences transcend geography and language in ways that surprise: despite vast cultural differences, there are common personality-music links that bridge continents.
The finding challenges the assumption that music taste is purely culturally constructed — there appear to be deeper, personality-driven patterns in what we're drawn to hearing.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Editorial: Inclusive leadership in multicultural teams: innovations, challenges and solutions - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Editorial: Inclusive leadership in multicultural teams: innovations, challenges and solutions  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — editorial pieces synthesise existing research but do not report primary findings. Applicability depends on the specific innovations and solutions discussed, which are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Inclusive leadership is a key lever for psychological safety in multicultural teams; identify how your current leadership practices create space for diverse voices and perspectives to be heard without fear of repercussions.

Multicultural team contexts present distinct psychological safety challenges — review whether your team's norms, communication practices, and conflict resolution processes are adapted for cultural differences in directness, hierarchy, and group harmony.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: High — large global sample across multiple countries and sectors, though representativeness depends on PwC's sampling methodology which is not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Identify which specific fears (job security, technology displacement, workload) are most prevalent in your workforce to tailor psychological safety interventions accordingly.
Use employee hopes data to design positive framing for organisational change initiatives — focusing on aspirations rather than threats can build psychological safety and engagement.
Compare your organisation's results against global benchmarks to diagnose gaps in psychological safety and prioritise where leader training or team interventions are needed most urgently.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on academic settings and multicultural teams; findings may not generalise to corporate or other organisational contexts. Geographic scope unclear from snippet provided.
takeaways: AI tools can be designed to support inclusive leadership practices that reduce gender bias in team dynamics; consider how algorithmic decision-support might flag or mitigate unconscious exclusion in multicultural settings.

Inclusive leadership in diverse teams requires intentional design — both human and algorithmic — to shape equitable outcomes; relying on AI alone risks automating existing biases unless paired with explicit inclusive leadership training.

Multicultural academic teams face compounded challenges (gender + cultural dynamics); AI-assisted approaches may help surface hidden patterns, but effectiveness depends on leadership commitment to psychological safety and equity.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - nature.com
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition — the mechanism (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression) is plausible across sectors, but findings are limited by unknown geographic scope, industry type, and sample size from the snippet alone.
takeaways: AI adoption without concurrent investment in psychological safety and ethical leadership may increase depression risk among employees — prioritise creating safe spaces for employees to voice concerns about AI tools and their impact.
Ethical leadership during AI rollout is not optional; it appears to be a protective factor that buffers the negative psychological effects of technological change.

Assess your team's psychological safety before and after AI implementation — use pulse surveys or focus groups to identify whether employees feel safe asking questions, admitting mistakes, or raising concerns about AI systems.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad application across geographies and sectors, though specific workforce composition and response rates are unclear from the snippet alone. As a PwC survey, findings likely skew toward professional and enterprise sectors.
takeaways: Use survey data on employee hopes and fears to benchmark psychological safety concerns in your own organisation — identify whether your team's top concerns align with global trends and prioritise interventions accordingly.

Design targeted safety interventions based on what the global workforce fears most — whether job security, AI disruption, or interpersonal conflict — to demonstrate organisational responsiveness and build trust.
Consider hope-based messaging alongside risk mitigation; employees' hopes can signal what they value most (e.g., growth, autonomy, purpose), which psychological safety initiatives can reinforce.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Limited — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience and client data, but specific sample composition, geographic scope, and methodology are unclear from the snippet provided. Findings may reflect practices among large multinational organisations that engage BCG.
takeaways: Create explicit norms and practices that make it safe for employees from underrepresented groups to speak up and contribute ideas without fear of judgment or retaliation — this levels participation across demographics.
Leaders should model vulnerability and respond non-defensively to questions or pushback; this signals that dissent is valued and reduces the perceived risk of speaking candidly.
Measure psychological safety regularly through anonymous surveys or focus groups to identify where barriers exist (e.g., specific teams or leadership styles) so you can target interventions.
